title.en: The Good Hunter and the Great Medicine

region.en: Battlefield where the good hunter fell, Seneca and Tuscarora country
region.zh: 善獵人倒下的戰場，塞內卡與塔斯卡洛拉之地

texts.period: Oldest version in Doty's History of Livingston County from an old Seneca via Mr. Horsford; ampler Tuscarora form in Elias Johnson 1881; transcribed by Beauchamp 1922

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'The Good Hunter and the Great Medicine'

summary.en: In ancient times a war broke out between two tribes. On the one side the forces were jointly led by a great warrior and a noted hunter - the good hunter, noted for kindness and generosity to all, even to beasts and birds, and considered their protector. The battle was going against his side, and as he turned to quit the field a heavy blow felled him; on recovering he found that he could as easily pass through as over the great tree that lay across his path, and at home his friends would not talk with him - he had been killed, and was present in spirit only. On the field lay his mortal part quite dead, and its scalp gone. A fox raised the death lament and called all the beasts together; they came by hundreds, vainly trying to revive their friend; the bear was asked to speak as the nearest relative and best friend of man, and appealed to each and all for medicine, but none did any good. The oriole called a council of the birds, from the eagle to the wren: the white-headed eagle said the dead would not revive unless the scalp was restored. The fox searched every bird's nest and every hen-roost in vain; the pigeon hawk flew too swiftly; the white heron stopped to feed on wild beans; at last the crow - whom the warrior with the scalp did not fear, for he was accustomed to her - saw the scalp stretched on its hoop to dry in the smoke above his cabin, and carried it off. But so dry and warped had it become that it would not fit, until the great eagle plucked one of his long feathers, dipped it in the mountain dew that had collected on his back, and applied it to the scalp. The scalp was placed on the head, to which it closely adhered; the hunter revived and recovered his strength, and they gave him the compound which had restored him, as the gift of the Great Spirit.
summary.zh: 上古兩族交戰，一方由大戰士與著名獵人共同統率——那「善獵人」對飛禽走獸無不仁慈，被視為它們的保護者。戰事失利，他轉身欲退，卻被重擊斃命；魂魄歸家，親友竟視而不見——他已身死，唯魂尚在。戰場上他的遺體橫陳，髮皮已被割去。狐哀號召集群獸，數以百計的野獸趕來相救而無效；熊以人類至親之名求眾獸獻藥，仍無一靈驗。金鶯又召百鳥之會，自鵰至鷦鷯雲集；白頭的老鵰說：除非尋回髮皮，死者不能復生。狐遍尋鳥巢雞舍無果；隼飛得太快；白鷺貪食野豆誤事；最後是烏鴉——割皮戰士素來不怕她——看見髮皮繃在籠上、懸於屋煙之上晾曬，便趁機攜走。但皮已乾翹不合頭顱；白頭鵰自背上凝結的山露中拔一根長羽蘸露敷之，髮皮遂潤而貼合。獵人復甦，恢復氣力；眾獸將救他的合藥作為大神之賜贈予他。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922 (Seneca via Horsford/Doty; Tuscarora via Elias Johnson 1881); public domain. Leland compares this to the Jesuit Relation's Ononhara feast of 1636; the panther (Ontarraoura) revived the good hunter 'in the midst of a good feast'.

passages.text: In ancient times a war broke out between two tribes. On the one side the forces were jointly led by a great warrior and a noted hunter. The latter had killed much game for the skins, the remains being left for beasts and birds of prey. The battle was going against his side, and he saw that, to save his own life, he must quit the field. As he turned, the body of a great tree lay across his path. He came up to it, when a heavy blow felled him. On recovering he found, strangely enough, that he could as easily pass through as over the obstruction. Reaching home, his friends would not talk with him; indeed they seemed quite unaware of his presence. It now occurred to him that he, too, had been killed, and was present in spirit only, human eyes not seeing him. He returned to the place of conflict, and there, sure enough, lay his mortal part quite dead, and its scalp gone.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 31-32; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: A pigeon hawk, flying by, recognized the disembodied hunter, and gratefully offered to restore his scalp; so, stretching away in its flight to the retiring victors, he plucked it from the bloody pole. The other birds had, meantime, prepared a medicine which soon united the scalp to the head, when bears and wolves gathered around and joined in the dance. The hunter got well and lived many years, his experience strengthening their religious faith, and teaching them how to use the remedies so strangely acquired, which, to this day, are among the most efficacious known to the Indians.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 31-32; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: A fox came along when the conflict was over, and recognized this friend of bird and beast lying lifeless on the field. Shocked by the sight he raised the death lament, and called all the beasts together. Their cries were heard in the forest; they came by hundreds to the spot and tried to revive their friend. Vain were all their efforts, and he remained lifeless... Then the bear was asked to speak, as being the nearest relative and best friend of man. He appealed to each and all for medicine, but though each had his own, none did any good... This sad lament brought the oriole to the spot. He was told of their sad plight, and in turn went and called a council of the birds. There was a flapping of wings everywhere, and all came, from the eagle to the wren, in response to the call... The eagle's head had become white in his long and wise life... This white-headed sage said that the dead would not revive unless the scalp was restored.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 32-33; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: At last the crow took up the mission. The warrior who had the scalp knew of the council, but feared nothing when he saw the crow flying near, for he was accustomed to that. She saw the scalp stretched on its hoop, to dry in the smoke above his cabin. Her chance came and she carried it off. Great was the rejoicing at her successful return. At once they put the scalp on his head, but so dry and warped had it become that it would not fit... Then the great eagle said that on the high rocks where he lived far above all other birds, the mountain dew had collected on his back, and perhaps this might serve. He plucked one of his long feathers, dipped it in this dew, and applied it to the scalp. It worked finely and the scalp was moist again... The scalp was placed on the head, to which it closely adhered. The hunter revived and recovered his strength. They gave him the compound which had restored him, as the gift of the Great Spirit, and there was then a pattering of feet and a rustle of wings as the council dispersed. The good hunter returned to his lodge in peace.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 33-34; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Plant That Heals Itself: The Medicine Found by Music
title.zh: 自癒之草：循歌聲覓得的藥

region.en: Forest path where the sweet music sounded

texts.period: Tuscarora chief Elias Johnson, Legends, Traditions and Laws of the Six Nations (1881), via Beauchamp 1922

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'The Medicine' (Elias Johnson's second medicine)

summary.en: One day a hunter heard the sweetest music in the woods, but thorough search did not reveal its source. Charmed by the sound he went again and again, but with no better success. Not a note was heard. At last the Great Spirit came to him in a dream and told him what to do. He was to purify himself before seeking it, and this he at once did. The forest path was taken, the charming strain fell upon his ear, and he listened attentively till he could sing every note himself. Then he drew nearer. A tall green plant stood before him, with long and tapering leaves. This he cut down, but it was immediately healed and became as before. He did this repeatedly with the same results, and then knew it as medicine especially good for wounds. Rejoicing in his great discovery, he took part of the plant home, where it was dried and pulverized. Then he touched it to a bad wound which a man had received, and it was healed at once. Thus did the Great Spirit give this great medicine to men, and very grateful were they for it.
summary.zh: 一日，獵人在林中聽見世上最甜美的樂聲，遍尋卻不見其源；他一再去聽，依舊一無所獲，連一個音符也聽不見。最後大神入夢指點：須先潔淨己身再去尋覓。他如儀淨身，重入林徑，仙樂入耳，他凝神諦聽直至自己能唱出每個音符。漸漸走近，一株高挑的綠草立在眼前，葉長而尖。他把它割倒，它卻立時癒合如初；屢割屢合，他這才知道這正是專治創傷的靈藥。他喜不自勝，取其一部分回家曬乾研末；觸於一處重傷之上，傷口立時癒合。大神便如此把這大藥賜給了人們。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922 (Johnson 1881); public domain. The plant's self-healing on being cut is the sign of its virtue.

title.en: The False Faces at the Onondaga Medicine Dance
title.zh: 奧農達加醫舞中的假臼者

region.en: Onondaga council house at the midwinter feast
region.zh: 奧農達加隆冬祭的議屋

texts.period: Observed by De Cost Smith, Jan. 26, 1883, at Onondaga; printed by Beauchamp 1922

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'False Faces' (De Cost Smith's account of the medicine dance)

summary.en: Though there have been medicine men of local reputation among the Onondagas, the False Faces have taken their place here in ceremonies for the sick. The members wear large wooden masks, the faces grotesquely carved and painted, the eyes adorned with brass or tin, and with horse hair for long flowing locks. If one dreamed he was a False Face, he related his dream to a proper person, and as Iroquois dreams must be fulfilled, he gave a feast and was initiated. All are males except one woman, who is Mistress of the Band - Go-go-sa Ho-nun-na-tase-ta, Keeper of the False Faces - who has charge of the regalia. The dance of Thursday, January 26th [1883] was a medicine dance, in which the Hon-do-i were not asked to help the people against the witches, but were expected, in view of the honor shown them, to withdraw the sickness for which they themselves were responsible. The head devil pushed open the door suddenly and entered with a bound to see if the feast were ready; when the food was declared cooked, the whole band of dancers entered and took seats near the middle of the room; the head chief threw tobacco into the fire, and lifting off the pot full of food gave it to the head devil, who took it and walked out, followed by the others; benches were arranged in a semi-circle in front of the women's stove, and those who were suffering from disease seated themselves to the number of thirty or forty; the False Faces ran their hands through the ashes on the hearth and, in single file around the half-circle of benches, each Hon-do-i in turn rubbing ashes upon the head of each of the sick persons - the action consisting in rubbing the hands quickly on the head, and then blowing upon it two or three times; a woman somewhat beyond middle age led out one of the sick women, while a man led forth one of the devils to dance with the patient, until each sick woman had danced with one of the devils.
summary.zh: 在奧農達加，為病人行禮的主事的已是「假臼者」社團。社員戴著巨大的木製面具，面相怪誕、塗繪斑斕，眼嵌銅錫，髮披馬鬃。凡夢見自己成為假臼者者，須把夢告知執禮之人——易洛魁之夢必須應驗——設宴而受入社禮。社中皆男子，唯有一位婦女為「假臼之守」戈戈薩霍南納塞塔，掌管法器。1883年1月26日的舞蹈是一場醫舞：不是請假臼者助人驅巫，而是他們受此尊崇之後，應自行收回其所致的疾病。大鬼猛地推門躍入查看宴席是否備妥；食物煮熟後，全隊入屋就座；大酋長向火中投菸草，舉起滿鍋食物交給大鬼，鬼隊隨之而出；病者三四十人列坐於弧形長凳，假臼者們以手攪動灶灰，列隊繞弧而行，逐一為病者以灰抹頭——其法為急搓頭頂兩三下、隨後向之吹氣；一位中年婦人引病婦出列，另一人引一位假臼者與病人對舞，直到每位病婦都與一位假臼者共舞一圈。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922 (De Cost Smith, JAFL 1888); public domain. An outside observer's 1883 ethnographic description of a living healing society; no ritual formulas disclosed.

passages.text: Though there have been medicine men of local reputation among the Onondagas, the False Faces have taken their place here in ceremonies for the sick. The members wear large wooden masks, the faces grotesquely carved and painted, the eyes adorned with brass or tin, and with horse hair for long flowing locks. Doorkeepers wear corn-husk masks here, but in Canada these form a distinct society. In the N. Y. Regents' Report for 1850, Mr. Lewis H. Morgan gives an account of them. The actual False Faces were properly evil spirits with supernatural powers, and without bodies or limb - really the traditional Flying Heads. They frequented solitary places, starting from tree to tree, paralyzing men and bringing storm and pestilence.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 36; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: As a society they appear in all Iroquois villages, having secret initiations, ceremonies and dances. If one dreamed he was a False Face, he related his dream to a proper person, and as Iroquois dreams must be fulfilled, he gave a feast and was initiated. If he dreamed he ceased to be a member, he gave a feast and withdrew. The dream governed throughout. When they appear in public as such, they all wear masks. All are males except one woman, who is Mistress of the Band. She is called Go-go-sa Ho-nun-na-tase-ta, or Keeper of the False Faces. She has charge of the regalia, and is the only organ of communication with the members, whose names are supposedly unknown.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 36; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: The dance of Thursday, January 26th, was more interesting, but was, properly speaking, a 'medicine dance,' in which the Hon-do-i were not asked to help the people against the witches, but were expected, in view of the honor shown them, to withdraw the sickness for which they themselves were responsible... During the early part of the day the dancers went from house to house, dancing for the cure of those who could not leave home. In the afternoon, toward three o'clock, the people gathered in the council house to await the coming of the Hon-do-i... the 'head devil' would push open the door suddenly and enter with a bound, to see if the feast were ready. When this had happened several times the food was declared cooked, and the whole band of dancers entered and took seats near the middle of the room.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 38-39; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: The head chief then stood up and addressed the dancers as A-gwe-ge, 'All.' Then proceeding to the stove, he threw tobacco into the fire, and lifting off the pot full of food gave it to the 'head devil,' who took it and walked out, followed by the others... On this semi-circle of benches those who were suffering from disease or sickness now seated themselves to the number of thirty or forty. When the devils had eaten the food they returned to the council house, and all save one... went to the stove, and with a great deal of grunting and groaning, 'Han-han, han-han,' ran their hands through the ashes on the hearth, and then started in single file around the half-circle of benches, each Hon-do-i in turn rubbing ashes upon the head of each of the sick persons. The action consists in rubbing the hands quickly on the head, and then blowing upon it two or three times... a man led forth one of the devils to dance with the patient. The pair, having danced facing each other to the other end of the row of benches, resumed their seats... until each sick woman had danced with one of the devils.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 38-39; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Stone Giant of Cardiff and the Covered Pitfall
title.zh: 卡迪夫的石巨人與陷坑之計

region.en: Near Cardiff, a little south of the Onondaga reservation
region.zh: 奧農達加保留地以南的卡迪夫附近

texts.period: Onondaga local tradition printed by Beauchamp 1922

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'Stonish Giants'

summary.en: The Onondagas have a local but different story. They say that a Stone Giant lived near Cardiff, a little south of their reservation. He was once like other men, but was a great eater, became a cannibal, and increased in size. His skin became hard and changed into scales, which alone would turn an arrow. Every day he came through the valley, caught and devoured an Onondaga, a fearful toll. The people were dismayed but formed a plan. They made a road in the marsh with a covered pitfall, decoyed the giant through the path and down he went and was killed. Of course when the Cardiff Giant was 'found' it did not astonish the Onondagas that he was of stone.
summary.zh: 奧農達加人另有一個本地故事：石巨人住在保留地以南不遠的卡迪夫附近。他本與常人無異，因為饕餮無度而食人，身軀日漸巨大；皮膚硬化成鱗，唯鱗甲能彈開箭矢。他每日穿谷而來，捉食一名奧農達加人，代價慘重。族人驚恐之餘定下計策：在沼澤中闢一條路，暗設覆草的陷坑，誘巨人循路而行——他一腳踏空，墜坑被誅。後來「卡迪夫石巨人」出土時，奧農達加人一點也不驚訝他竟是石頭做的。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922; public domain. The famous 1869 Cardiff Giant hoax is here folded into Onondaga tradition.

passages.text: The Onondagas have a local but different story. They say that a Stone Giant lived near Cardiff, a little south of their reservation, which is by no means their early home. He was once like other men, but was a great eater, became a cannibal, and increased in size. His skin became hard and changed into scales, which alone would turn an arrow. Every day he came through the valley, caught and devoured an Onondaga, a fearful toll.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 40-41; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: The people were dismayed but formed a plan. They made a road in the marsh with a covered pitfall, decoyed the giant through the path and down he went and was killed. Of course when the Cardiff Giant was 'found' it did not astonish the Onondagas that he was of stone.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 41; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Stone Giant's Race at Green Pond and the Bone Pointer

region.en: Green Pond hollow west of Jamesville, where the rocks rise 200 feet on three sides
region.zh: 詹姆斯維爾以西的綠池窪地，三面絕壁高二百呎

texts.period: Onondaga local tradition (Beauchamp 1922); 'one of the oldest Stone Giant stories, closely resembling one told by David Cusick'

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'Stonish Giants' (the Jamesville race)

summary.en: The Onondagas have also a story of a Stone Giant's race with a man near Jamesville. He ran the man into the hollow at Green Pond, west of that village, where the rocks rise 200 feet above the water on three sides. On the south side the precipice can be ascended by a natural stairway at one spot, and the man was far enough ahead to reach the top before the other. He lay down and looked from the rocks to see what the other would do. The latter came and looked around. Not seeing the man he took out of his pouch what seemed a finger, but was really a pointer of bone. By means of this he could find any object he wished, and so it was always useful in hunting. As he climbed the rocks the man reached down and took away the pointer before the other saw him. The giant begged him to restore it: if he would do this he was promised good luck and long life for himself and friends. Though he begged so piteously the man ran home with it to show his friends, leaving him there helpless, unable to find his way. His friends interceded, telling him to accept the giant's good offer and not incur his enmity. So they went back and found him still at the lake. He received his pointer, promising to eat men no more, and good luck followed the man.
summary.zh: 奧農達加人還有一則石巨人與人在詹姆斯維爾附近賽跑的故事。巨人把那人追進村西的綠池窪地——三面絕壁高二百呎；南壁有一處天然石階，那人領先足以先登頂。他伏在岩上俯視對手的動靜。巨人尋人不見，便自囊中取出一物，看似手指，其實是骨製的指針：憑它可尋得任何物件，打獵時最是有用。他攀岩之際，那人俯身奪走指針。巨人苦苦哀求歸還：若肯還他，他允諾賜那人及其親友福壽綿長。那人不顧哀告，攜針跑回家向朋友誇示，把巨人丟在原地無路可尋。親友勸他莫結仇怨、領受巨人的好意；眾人折返，見巨人仍在湖邊。他交還指針，巨人允諾從此不再食人；福運自此伴隨那人。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922; public domain. Same pointer motif as Cusick's Stonish Giant tale and Parker's Animated Finger.

title.en: The Pigmy Feast and the Dance in Darkness
title.zh: 小人祭宴與黑暗中的舞蹈

region.en: Caves in rocky places of the Grand River country
region.zh: 格蘭德河之地岩穴中的小人族

texts.period: Related by David Boyle (Grand River, Canada), printed by Beauchamp 1922

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'Indian Fairies' (Boyle's account of the pigmy dance)

summary.en: A race of small people is believed to inhabit caves in rocky places. These people did not appear till long after the creation of the Indians, and are quite different from them in disposition, as well as in size and appearance. Scarcely more than three feet high and of a pale yellow color, they dressed 'all over,' even in summer time, differing in this respect from the Indian. They are not credited with any mischievous tendencies, but were rather disposed to assist the hunter in pursuit of his game. To secure the good offices of the pigmies, however, it was necessary that a feast should be given in their honor: in the old days the custom was to kill the first deer for this purpose, and as the pigmies were particularly fond of corn soup, this dish formed a prominent feature of the feast. Thirty-six songs are peculiar to this ceremony, during the first part of which, these, with four exceptions, are sung in accompaniment to the women's dance, in perfect darkness. Wherever a pigmy feast is given, all these songs must be sung, one-half of them by the men and one-half by the women. No rattle is employed in these dances, but a drum in the hands of a man is constantly in use... At the conclusion of this second part the room is lighted and the remaining four songs are sung by the women, who dance by moving in a circle in the usual way, while the dance engaged in when the room was dark consisted of a slight alternate shuffle forwards and backwards. My informant gave it as his opinion that the portion of the ceremony performed in darkness referred to the doubt and difficulty connected with an unsuccessful hunt, while the lighting up symbolized the capture of game.
summary.zh: 相傳有一族小人居於岩穴之中。他們在印第安人受造之後很久方才出現，性情、身量、外貌皆與印第安人迥異：身高不足三呎、膚色淡黃，連盛夏也「全身」著衣。他們並無惡作劇之名，反而樂於助獵人追捕獵物。要得小人相助，須為他們設祭：古俗是射殺的第一頭鹿即為此用；小人最愛玉米湯，此菜為祭宴之主。這場儀式專有三十六首歌：前半段除四首外皆伴女子之舞於全黑之中唱出；凡舉小人祭，三十六歌必須全唱，男女各半；舞不用鈴，唯男子執鼓不輟。第二段結束時屋內點燈，餘下四首由女子唱出，她們如常繞圈起舞——黑暗中的舞步只是前後輕輕挪移。講述者以為：黑暗中行禮，喻獵之無獲與艱難；點燈之時，喻獵物到手。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922 (Boyle); public domain. The Mohawks call the pigmies Yagodinenyoyaks, Stone Throwers.

passages.text: A race of small people is believed to inhabit caves in rocky places. These people did not appear till long after the creation of the Indians, and are quite different from them in disposition, as well as in size and appearance. Scarcely more than three feet high and of a pale yellow color, they dressed 'all over,' even in summer time, differing in this respect from the Indian. They are not credited with any mischievous tendencies, but were rather disposed to assist the hunter in pursuit of his game. To secure the good offices of the pigmies, however, it was, as a matter of course, necessary that a feast should be given in their honor. In the old days the custom was to kill the first deer for this purpose, and as the pigmies were particularly fond of corn soup, this dish formed a prominent feature of the feast.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 42; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Thirty-six songs are peculiar to this ceremony, during the first part of which, these, with four exceptions, are sung in accompaniment to the women's dance, in perfect darkness. Wherever a pigmy feast is given, all these songs must be sung, one-half of them by the men and one-half by the women. No rattle is employed in these dances, but a drum in the hands of a man is constantly in use. After the men have sung their sixteen songs, the women do their half of the singing, continuing to dance at the same time. At the conclusion of this second part the room is lighted and the remaining four songs are sung by the women, who dance by moving in a circle in the usual way, while the dance engaged in when the room was dark consisted of a slight alternate shuffle forwards and backwards, the dancers remaining in one place. The pigmy dance requires about an hour and a half, and is usually held in the house of the man or woman who gives the feast.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, p. 42; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: My informant gave it as his opinion that the portion of the ceremony performed in darkness referred to the doubt and difficulty connected with an unsuccessful hunt, while the lighting up symbolized the capture of game. In accordance with the Mohawk myth, as held by some, the pigmies are fond of playing pranks by throwing stones, hence the name - Yagodinenyoyaks, Stone Throwers.
passages.note: Verbatim from Beauchamp 1922, pp. 42-43; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Little Old Woman and the Three Gifts

region.en: Between Mohawk and Palatine Bridge, Mohawk Valley
region.zh: 莫霍克與帕拉廷橋之間的莫霍克河谷

texts.period: Told by Rev. Thomas La Fort, Onondaga Wesleyan minister, 1899 (Beauchamp 1922)

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'Indian Fairies' (La Fort's tale of the stone-throwers)

summary.en: By our forefathers it has been related that long, long ago, there lived between Mohawk and Palatine Bridge very little folks. They lived by themselves and were called 'stone-throwers.' I, Thomas La Fort, saw such a one about thirty years ago, when I was traveling on the road to Albany; he sat on top of a hill and looked down on the road. These little men could appear and disappear whenever they wished. About 200 years ago there was a poor man, running around hunting in the woods, but unable to kill a deer. So he was feeling very badly and very hungry, when suddenly he saw a very little old woman standing before him, who said she had been waiting for him and could make him very happy. She offered him three different things: (1) He could find precious gold; (2) He could find bright silver; (3) He could kill as many deer as he wished, having the power to call the animals to him. Then she told him he would enjoy the venison which he would find on the shelves of his wigwam. It happened as the little woman had said, he could shoot the deer without trouble, for they came to him when he called.
summary.zh: 祖先相傳：很久很久以前，莫霍克與帕拉廷橋之間住著一群小小的人。他們自成一部，人稱「擲石者」。我托馬斯拉福特約三十年前赴奧爾巴尼途中親見其一——他坐在山頂俯望大路。這些小人可隨意隱現。約二百年前，有個窮苦的獵人在林中奔走卻獵不到鹿，又餓又難過。忽然一位極矮小的老嫗立在他面前，說已等候多時，能叫他快活起來。她許他三樣東西任選：一、可以尋得貴重的黃金；二、可以尋得閃亮的白銀；三、可以隨心所欲地獵鹿——有呼獸即至的本領。她又說他將在自家棚架上看見掛好的鹿肉。果如小老嫗所言，他喚鹿鹿至，射之不費吹灰之力。

title.en: The Bone Comb: Do Not Look Back

region.en: The road where the little woman met the grandmother and child
region.zh: 小老嫗遇祖孫二人的大路

texts.period: Told by Rev. Thomas La Fort (Beauchamp 1922)

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'Indian Fairies' (the bone comb tale)

summary.en: When I was a boy my grandmother told me that she had a grandchild who once was walking with her great grandmother on a road, the grandchild going ahead. Suddenly there appeared a strange-looking little woman, who spoke to her and said, 'You are feeling unhappy because you cannot walk as steadily as in your younger days, and yet you may become young again, providing you will do as I tell you. Tell your grandchild to walk straight ahead, and not to look back until I give her permission.' The grandmother did as she was bidden, and the little woman took a bone comb out of her pocket and said, 'Comb your hair with this as far as your hands can extend.' The old woman noticed that her hair was lengthening as far as she could reach, at the same time her skin changed color rapidly, when suddenly the grandchild looked back, and her grandmother, saying, 'My dear child you have destroyed me,' fell down dead.
summary.zh: 我幼時聽祖母講過：她的孫女曾與曾祖母同行，孫女在前。忽然一位模样奇異的小婦現身對老太太說：「你正為步履不再穩健而鬱鬱；但只要你照我說的做，便可重返青春。叫你的孫女一直朝前走，未經我允許不可回頭。」老太太依言行事；小婦自囊中取出一把骨梳：「用它梳頭，梳到你手能伸到之處。」老太太只覺秀髮隨梳而長，膚色瞬息轉變——孫女卻忽然回頭。老太太說聲「我的孩子，你害了我」，倒地而亡。

title.en: The Invisible Fingers and the Twelve Pairs of Moccasins
title.zh: 看不見的手與十二雙鹿皮鞋

region.en: Lone lodge where the sick youth lay while the village was sugar-making
region.zh: 村人熬糖時病童獨臥的孤屋

texts.period: Told by Rev. Thomas La Fort not long before his death (Beauchamp 1922)

source.work: W. M. Beauchamp, Iroquois Folk Lore (1922), 'Indian Fairies' (La Fort's moccasin-maker tale)

summary.en: While all the Onondagas were once off sugar-making, a young man remained at home alone because he was ill. While lying on his couch he felt fingers stroking his forehead. Then they patted his shoulders, but no one was seen. Then they came down his arm, and a small arm appeared, but no body. He seized the arm with all his might, but could not hold it, and received a blow upon his head. Then all was still. His mother came home and he told her all this. 'O, my son,' said she, 'You have done very wrong. You have driven away your best friend, but I will try to make amends. To-night I will take a good deer's hide and cut it in pieces for twelve pairs of moccasins. This I will put in a convenient place, and lay with it beads, thread and colored moose hair.' This she did. At midnight the young man heard a noise and felt the fingers, as before, but kept still. Then the fingers went away and he heard a sound where the deer-skin lay. In the morning all was gone. The next night came and nothing was heard, but in the morning there stood a pair of moccasins, beautiful beyond anything Onondaga had ever seen. The sick youth was soon well.
summary.zh: 奧農達加人傾村熬糖之時，一個生病的青年獨自留守家中。他臥在榻上，覺得有手指撫弄他的額頭；接著拍他的肩，卻不見人影；又順著他的手臂而下，現出一條小臂，卻沒有身子。他用力去抓，卻抓不住，反捱了一記腦門。此後一片寂靜。母親回來聽了原委：「兒啊，你錯了。你把最好的朋友趕走了；讓我設法補救。今夜我取一張好鹿皮，裁成十二雙鞋料，連同珠子、線和染色駝鹿毛一併放在方便之處。」她如言備齊。半夜青年又聞響動、覺得手指拂來，這回他屏息不動；手指離去，鹿皮處沙沙作響。清晨皮料盡失。次日夜裡無聲無息，晨起卻立著一雙鹿皮鞋——精美絕倫，奧農達加前所未見。病青年的病也很快好了。

sensitivity.note: Beauchamp 1922 (La Fort); public domain. Such things, La Fort said, used to be frequent in the old times; since Christianity prevailed they had disappeared.
